items.headline: Warsh: Fed's role on AI is 'neither advocacy nor opposition'
items.take: In his Nov. 16 remarks at the Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, Chairman Warsh said the Fed's role is 'neither advocacy nor opposition' and that widespread adoption of the technology 'will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road.' He said the big questions are about 'magnitude, scope, and timing.' AlphaGen read: the Fed is framing AI as something to measure and plan for rather than a stance to take.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (Warsh opening remarks, Nov. 16, 2026)

items.headline: Warsh: if AI broadens idea generation, growth could stay above long-run average
items.take: Warsh said 'super intelligence' might differ from past general-purpose technologies because it 'could supercharge idea generation,' adding that 'if idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average.' He also said 'we're certainly not here to make predictions.' AlphaGen read: the claim is explicitly conditional, in line with his description of staff scenarios as illustrative, not forecasts.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (Warsh opening remarks, Nov. 16, 2026)

items.headline: Waller: in payments, trust is measured 'in years and even decades'
items.take: In a Nov. 17 speech to The Clearing House Annual Conference in New York on payments and tokenized markets, Governor Waller said "In payments, trust is measured not in months and quarters, but in years and even decades." He added that "Tokenization is still in the early innings of robust competition among new entrants, established firms, and combinations of each." AlphaGen read: the framing stresses reliability over speed of innovation.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Waller speech

items.headline: Waller sees several tokenization solutions; Fed to provide core settlement infrastructure
items.take: Governor Waller said in his Nov. 17 speech: "I find it more likely that several different solutions will emerge to support different customers and use cases." He also said "The Federal Reserve can support these solutions by providing core payment and settlement infrastructure upon which the private sector can innovate." AlphaGen read: the speech positions the Fed as infrastructure provider rather than product designer.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Waller speech

items.headline: Waller cites Binance events as showing issues programmable blockchains can raise
items.take: Governor Waller said in his Nov. 17 payments speech that "The recent events around Binance have highlighted some of the issues that can arise from programmable blockchains," and that "systemically important financial transactions may call for the most conservative designs." He also said new tokenized services "will need more than just technical prowess." AlphaGen read: the remarks tie crypto-market incidents to design standards for systemically important payments.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Waller speech

items.take: Diamondback said its first full-section Barnett development, at Spanish Trail in Midland County, consists of four 10,000-foot lateral wells that at a recent peak produced approximately 7.5 MBo/d and 37 MMcf/d. items.take: BLS's October PPI release shows final demand changes of +0.6, +0.5, +0.8, +1.1, +0.5, -0.1, +0.1, +0.4, +1.4 and +0.3 percent for January through October, with June the only decline. Compounding those published, rounded figures gives roughly 5.7% over the ten months, against a 12-month change of 6.5% for the period ended in October. AlphaGen read: March (+0.8%), April (+1.1%) and September (+1.4%) were the three largest monthly gains, so the cumulative figure is driven by a few large months rather than a steady drift.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: PPI final demand energy: four declines in 2026, but monthly changes compound to ~34%
items.take: BLS's October PPI table shows final demand energy changing -1.7, +2.0, +10.5, +7.1, +8.2, -7.2, -1.5, +4.2, +10.0 and -0.1 percent from January through October. Four of the ten months were declines, and six were gains of 2.0% or more. Compounding the published, rounded monthly figures gives roughly 34.4% over the ten months. AlphaGen read: March (+10.5%) and September (+10.0%) were the two largest monthly moves, which dominates the compounded total.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: PPI transportation and warehousing services: six of ten 2026 months rose 2% or more
items.take: In BLS's October PPI table, final demand transportation and warehousing services changed +1.0, +0.8, +2.2, +3.7, +2.1, -0.3, -1.1, +2.4, +3.4 and +2.0 percent from January through October. Six months were gains of 2.0% or more and two were declines (June and July). Compounding the published, rounded figures gives roughly 17.3% over the ten months. AlphaGen read: October's +2.0% is the third straight gain of that size after the June-July dip.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: PPI final demand foods rose 1.3% in October, the largest monthly gain since February
items.take: BLS's October PPI table shows final demand foods up 1.3% in October after +1.1% in September, versus +2.3% in February; the other seven 2026 months ranged from -1.3% to +0.6%. Five of the ten months were declines, and compounding the published, rounded changes gives roughly +2.0% for January through October. AlphaGen read: foods compounded to about 2.0% against about 34.4% for energy, though the last two months have turned upward.

items.take: BEA said the increase in Q3 investment primarily reflected private inventory investment and equipment. The largest contributors to inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing, both led by nondurable goods industries, based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data. AlphaGen read: inventories and equipment are the two named drivers of the Q3 investment increase behind 3.4% real GDP growth at an annual rate; BEA's second estimate is due Nov. 25.

items.take: BLS reported average hourly earnings for all private nonfarm employees rose 14 cents, or 0.4%, to $38.00 in October, and are up 3.1% over the past 12 months. For production and nonsupervisory employees, hourly earnings rose 12 cents, or 0.4%, to $32.75. items.headline: ECB's Vujčić: IPO volumes on track to exceed dot-com high relative to U.S. GDP
items.take: In his Nov. 16 Euro Finance Week speech, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić said equity issuance is surging, with IPO volumes now on track to exceed the dot-com bubble high relative to U.S. GDP. He added that such surges have historically often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism. AlphaGen read: the ECB is treating issuance volume itself, not just valuations, as a stability signal.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: ECB publishes its Financial Stability Review two days after Nov. 16 speech
items.take: Vujčić said the ECB publishes its latest Financial Stability Review two days after his Nov. 16 remarks, and that an early-release special feature on AI-related cyber capabilities and concentration of ICT third-party providers was published that day. He named AI and sovereign debt markets as the two risks that stand out most versus a year ago. AlphaGen read: the full review lands this week and should expand on both themes.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: euro-area underlying inflation stable, wages not responding materially yet
items.take: Vujčić said euro-area headline inflation rose to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, mainly on energy, while underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. He said weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain the energy-driven rise by weighing on growth. AlphaGen read: the ECB is separating an energy shock from broader price-setting.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić flags leveraged hedge funds in sovereign bond markets, Japanese investor risk
items.take: Vujčić said hedge funds have become a significant but procyclical source of liquidity in sovereign bond markets, and that large Japanese investors may further reduce euro-area government bond holdings if Japanese yields rise. He said the growing footprint of leveraged hedge funds creates additional vulnerabilities. AlphaGen read: the ECB sees the buyer base for sovereign debt as increasingly price-sensitive.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Warsh: research effort up 20x+ since the 1930s, yet research productivity fell more
items.take: Opening the Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference on Nov. 16, Chairman Warsh cited estimates that research efforts have increased more than 20 times since the 1930s, while, quoting Bloom, Jones and coauthors, research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount. He said productivity growth has been reasonably strong in recent quarters but has not broken out definitively to the upside. AlphaGen read: the Chair is framing the AI debate around idea generation, not just capital spending.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: 4-week bill high rate 4.068% on Oct. 15, up 2.0 bp from 4.048% a week earlier
items.take: Treasury results show the $110 billion 4-week bill auctioned Oct. 15 had a 4.068% high investment rate and a 2.56 bid-to-cover ratio, versus 4.048% and 2.40 for the $110 billion offering on Oct. 8. The 8-week bill on Oct. 15 cleared at 4.132% with a 2.26 bid-to-cover. AlphaGen read: demand at the front end firmed slightly for the 4-week even as the rate edged up.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: Elderson: ECB aims to cut small banks' reporting to about 5% of large banks' data points
items.take: In a Nov. 16 opinion piece, the ECB's Frank Elderson said the ECB and the European Banking Authority are pursuing reforms that should ultimately reduce reporting by small and non-complex banks to around 5% of the data points reported by large banks. He said supervisors could also run stress-test projections centrally, lightening the workload for almost 1,000 institutions, while stressing that proportionality cannot mean lower standards. AlphaGen read: the ECB is pairing simpler reporting with an explicit safety-and-soundness caveat.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Barr flags fast chip depreciation risk; older-vintage lease rates 'holding up'
items.take: Governor Barr said the bulk of a data center's cost comes from GPUs and other specialized chips, and one concern is that they may depreciate quickly as newer technologies overtake them, leaving capacity of little future use. He said lease rates of older chip vintages currently appear to be holding up, suggesting uses even for older computing technology. AlphaGen read: collateral values of GPU-backed financings depend on how long older chips stay in demand.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: equity-strategy leverage has risen, with prime brokers at large dealers a channel
items.take: Governor Barr said leverage at hedge funds and risk appetite appear quite high, so a sharp reversal could lead to rapid deleveraging and self-reinforcing fire sales, and that leverage used in equity strategies has also increased in recent years, provided in part via large dealers' prime brokerage. He said high capital at the largest banks is a bulwark against spillovers but counterparty exposures could rise in a period of equity-market volatility. AlphaGen read: the Fed's concern centers on the leveraged-fund channel rather than direct AI-related losses.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: equity premium low versus history, though not as low as the dot-com peak
items.take: Governor Barr said the equity premium, a rough measure of the extra return investors require for holding stocks over risk-free bonds, is at low levels relative to historical norms, though not nearly as low as in the dot-com boom. He noted the Fed does not target financial-market levels and called the premium one indicator among several of valuations. AlphaGen read: the Fed is framing valuations as a financial-stability input, not a market call.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: hyperscaler capex and debt yet to surpass the 1990s telecom cycle, but may soon
items.take: Governor Barr said the Fed's Financial Stability Report compares hyperscalers' cumulative capital spending and debt issuance since 2020 with those of all telecommunications firms during the broadband cycle that began in 1995. He said hyperscalers have yet to surpass their comparators, but the recent acceleration in capital expenditures suggests they may do so soon. AlphaGen read: the Fed is using the telecom buildout as its reference case for a debt-funded technology cycle.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: Fed's FSR puts hyperscaler off-balance-sheet obligations above $3 trillion
items.take: In his Nov. 16 Milan speech, Fed Governor Michael Barr said the Financial Stability Report estimates the potential maximum nominal value of hyperscalers' long-term contracts, lease commitments and residual value guarantees now exceeds $3 trillion. He said these have grown even more rapidly than on-balance-sheet debt and that the opacity of such structures can exacerbate selloffs, so they warrant close monitoring. AlphaGen read: the Fed is flagging contingent AI-related commitments, not just reported debt, as the place risk could hide.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Vujčić: sovereign debt fragilities rising on both sides of the Atlantic
items.take: In his Nov. 16 Euro Finance Week keynote, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić said sovereign debt fragilities have further increased on both sides of the Atlantic and are among the factors driving up long-term yields. He said hedge funds have become a significant but procyclical source of liquidity, and that large Japanese investors may further reduce euro area government bond holdings if Japanese yields rise. AlphaGen read: the ECB is linking bond-market supply and investor-base shifts to financial stability.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić asks if AI debt issuance could crowd out other borrowers
items.take: Vujčić said the substantial financing needs of the AI investment boom raise questions about competition for capital between public and private borrowers, including whether AI-related debt issuance could put upward pressure on financing costs or crowd out other investment. He also said firms are increasingly relying on opaque off-balance-sheet financing structures and circular financial arrangements. AlphaGen read: the ECB is treating AI funding as a credit-market issue, not only an equity one.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: private credit's rapid growth warrants close monitoring
items.take: Vujčić said private credit can diversify financing sources for firms and that risks currently appear contained, but its rapid growth warrants close monitoring given limited transparency, growing interconnectedness with banks and insurers, and potential liquidity mismatches. He said tools to address systemic risks in the non-bank sector remain limited compared with banking. AlphaGen read: the ECB is pressing for a system-wide framework for non-bank finance.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: euro-area bank capital buffers not a binding lending constraint
items.take: Vujčić said euro-area banks have maintained strong capital and liquidity positions, supported by solid profitability and retained earnings, and that current regulatory capital buffers do not appear to be a binding constraint on lending. He said they should be preserved as insurance against future shocks. He added that the Financial Stability Review is due two days after the speech. AlphaGen read: the ECB is signaling no appetite to loosen buffers.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Elderson: ECB backs raising small-bank threshold to €10bn, adding about 150 banks
items.take: ECB Executive Board member Frank Elderson wrote on Nov. 16 that the small and non-complex bank framework requires a balance sheet below €5 billion today, and that amending the regulation to let national authorities raise it to €10 billion would, with a redefinition of non-complex, bring about 150 more banks under it. He said joint reforms with the EBA should ultimately reduce reporting by such banks to around 5% of the data points reported by large banks. AlphaGen read: this is a proposal, and he stressed that proportionality cannot mean lower standards.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread 0.27 point on Nov. 13, from 0.38 on Nov. 5
items.take: FRED shows the 10-year minus 2-year Treasury constant-maturity spread at 0.27 percentage point on Nov. 13, up 0.03 from 0.24 on Nov. 12 and down 0.11 from 0.38 on Nov. 5. AlphaGen read: the curve is still positively sloped but flatter than at the start of the month.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Warsh calls "super intelligence" a general-purpose technology that demands Fed attention
items.take: Opening the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco, Chairman Warsh called the arrival of "super intelligence" an "entirely new force in economic life and society." He said the Fed's role is "neither advocacy nor opposition," but that wide adoption will have significant impact on the economy, with implications for monetary policy "down the road." AlphaGen read: the Chairman is framing AI as a policy input to plan for, not a call on rates.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh: productivity growth "reasonably strong" lately but no definitive breakout yet
items.take: Chairman Warsh said productivity growth has fluctuated and, in recent quarters, "it's been reasonably strong," but "it hasn't yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside." He cited Bloom, Jones and coauthors: research efforts have increased more than 20 times since the 1930s, yet research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount. AlphaGen read: the Chairman did not claim an AI productivity boom is yet visible in the data.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh outlines three illustrative AI scenarios Fed staff are modeling, "not forecasts"
items.take: Chairman Warsh said Board staff have begun evaluating contingencies with stylized, model-based frameworks: broadly shared gains with real GDP growth persistently above its long-run average; labor market disruption that could push the jobless rate above levels consistent with full employment; or a disappointment in which equity valuations fall, bringing a slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment. He called them "illustrative scenarios, not forecasts." AlphaGen read: the spread of outcomes shows why the Fed describes this as planning rather than predicting.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh: Productivity and Jobs panel is one of five task forces he has convened
items.take: Chairman Warsh said the Productivity and Jobs Task Force is "one of five" he has convened as Chairman, meant to take discussion "further and deeper than fleeting data points or daily market moves." He called the groups an intellectual investment to better equip the Fed "for the next policy conjuncture and beyond," under the theme "One Fed. Fit for Purpose. Focused on the Future." AlphaGen read: the task forces signal a longer-horizon framing alongside meeting-by-meeting data.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh flags AI risks to critical infrastructure, including from "bad actors"
items.take: Chairman Warsh said "great opportunities rarely come risk free," noting that super intelligence "empowers all, including bad actors," and that the Fed is thinking especially of "critical infrastructures and their potential vulnerabilities." He posed open questions on magnitude, scope and timing, including whether total factor productivity will rise and when any surge would start and taper. AlphaGen read: the speech raises questions rather than answers, consistent with his statement that the Fed is "certainly not here to make predictions."
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Bank of Canada Governor Macklem will not seek a second term; term ends June 2, 2027
items.take: The Bank of Canada said Governor Tiff Macklem told its Board he will not seek a second term when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027. The Board's independent directors have formed a Search Committee, with the process expected to be completed by spring 2027 and the next Governor's seven-year term set to begin June 3, 2027, subject to approval by the Minister of Finance and Cabinet. AlphaGen read: the announcement sets a long runway for a handover at Canada's central bank.
items.source_name: Bank of Canada

items.headline: ECB's Vujčić: euro-area headline inflation rose to 4% in October from 3.8%
items.take: In a Nov. 16 keynote at Euro Finance Week, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić said headline inflation in the euro area increased to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, mainly due to higher energy prices, while underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. He added that weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain inflation by weighing on growth. AlphaGen read: the ECB is describing an energy-driven rise rather than a broad one.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: ECB's Vujčić: US tech capex seen at $5.5 trillion by 2030, AI debt issuance at record
items.take: Vujčić said large cloud and AI infrastructure providers are increasingly turning to debt markets, with issuance volumes reaching record highs this year, and that cumulative capital expenditure by major US technology firms is projected to reach USD 5.5 trillion by 2030. He also said IPO volumes are on track to exceed the dot-com bubble high relative to US GDP. AlphaGen read: the ECB is flagging AI funding as a financial-stability topic, alongside sovereign debt, ahead of its Financial Stability Review two days later.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: ECB's Elderson: about 75% of nationally supervised euro banks are small and non-complex
items.take: In a Nov. 16 contribution for Börsen-Zeitung, ECB Executive Board member Frank Elderson wrote that around 75% of banks supervised by national authorities in the euro area, more than 1,400 institutions, qualify as small and non-complex, with the share at 81% in Germany. Such banks need only report up to 30% of the data reported by larger counterparts. AlphaGen read: the ECB and national supervisors have set out proposals to make oversight of smaller banks more risk-focused without lowering safety standards.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Barr: AI firms' on-balance-sheet debt expected to exceed $800 billion by year-end
items.take: Fed Governor Michael Barr said in Milan on Nov. 16 that on-balance-sheet debt of the seven largest AI firms has been growing significantly in 2026 and is expected to exceed $800 billion before year's end. He cited the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, which estimates the potential maximum nominal value of off-balance-sheet liabilities now exceeds $3 trillion. AlphaGen read: the "potential maximum" wording means the $3 trillion is an upper bound on obligations, not a loss estimate.

items.headline: Barr "less concerned about direct losses" from AI boom, flags fire-sale risk
items.take: Governor Barr said that, given the still-limited amount of debt backing the current boom, he is less concerned about direct losses. He added that with leverage at hedge funds and broader risk appetite apparently quite high, a sharp reversal could lead to rapid deleveraging and, potentially, self-reinforcing fire sales. AlphaGen read: his worry is the transmission channel through leveraged holders, not the size of AI debt itself.

items.headline: EIA: Flaming Gorge water released to protect Lake Powell power; Hoover Dam exposed
items.take: EIA's Nov. 13 analysis says water was released from Flaming Gorge, in the Upper Colorado River Basin, to reduce the risk of Lake Powell falling below the minimum power pool at Glen Canyon Dam. EIA adds that lower releases from Lake Powell could affect water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. AlphaGen read: the two reservoirs are linked, so protecting one shifts the risk to the other.

items.take: EIA's Nov. 13 analysis says this year's El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast for the Southwest. EIA cautions, however, that one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. AlphaGen read: the agency's own forecast does not yet count on a rebound, with 2027 Southwest hydropower at 6.1 billion kWh versus 6.13 billion kWh in 2026.

items.take: Jefferson said firms and workers will likely broaden and intensify their use of AI and reorganize production and workflows, and that successful firms could gain a competitive advantage, enabling them to expand and draw labor and capital away from competing firms. items.take: Citing one recent study, Jefferson said most adopting firms use AI in at most a few business functions, most commonly sales and marketing, strategy and business development, and information technology. He said it likely reflects a variety of factors, including a pickup in new business formation, and that teasing out AI's contribution is not straightforward. Capital goods increased $3.8 billion and foods, feeds and beverages $1.9 billion (soybeans up $1.3 billion), while nonmonetary gold fell $3.4 billion and crude oil rose $1.2 billion. Services exports added $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion. AlphaGen read: capital goods and agricultural products led the increase, with gold the main offset.
items.source_name: BEA and Census Bureau, U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026

items.headline: Real goods deficit widened 3.0% to $119.5B in Sept, faster than the 2.2% nominal rise
items.take: On a Census basis in 2017 dollars, the real goods deficit increased $3.5 billion, or 3.0 percent, to $119.5 billion in September, versus a 2.2 percent increase in the nominal deficit. Real goods exports rose 0.1 percent to $152.2 billion against a 2.5 percent nominal gain, while real imports rose 1.4 percent to $271.6 billion against 2.4 percent nominal. AlphaGen read: in volume terms, export growth was far smaller than the nominal figures suggest.
items.source_name: BEA and Census Bureau, U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026

items.headline: Sept trade: Canada deficit narrowed $2.7B to $4.4B; EU widened $3.2B, Taiwan $3.6B
items.take: BEA reported the September goods deficit with Canada decreased $2.7 billion to $4.4 billion, as exports fell $0.3 billion to $29.7 billion and imports fell $3.0 billion to $34.1 billion. The deficit with the European Union increased $3.2 billion to $14.2 billion (exports $39.0 billion, imports $53.2 billion), and the Taiwan deficit increased $3.6 billion to $21.9 billion on imports of $27.3 billion. AlphaGen read: the month's country moves ran in opposite directions, with Canada narrowing while the EU and Taiwan widened.
items.source_name: BEA and Census Bureau, U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026

items.headline: BEA: Q3 export drop was led by petroleum; capital goods the biggest import contributor
items.take: BEA's advance estimate put third-quarter real GDP growth at 3.4 percent, with a decrease in exports offsetting part of the gain while imports, a subtraction in GDP, increased. BEA said the export decrease primarily reflected goods, led by petroleum and related products, and that the largest contributor to imports was capital goods other than automotive. The second estimate is due Nov. 25. AlphaGen read: the trade drag in Q3 traced to energy exports and equipment imports, not a broad fall in goods trade.
items.source_name: Bureau of Economic Analysis, GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026

items.take: In his Nov. 12 Yale speech, Governor Barr said the top 0.1% of households, about 135,000 individuals and families, own one-sixth of U.S. wealth, citing the Fed's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. He put the entry point to the top 1% at $16.3 million, 75 times the $215,000 of a household in the middle, and said private equity makes up 12% of the top 0.1%'s assets. AlphaGen read: the speech treats distribution as context for how the economy responds to AI rather than as a rates signal.

items.headline: Barr names three drivers of the falling labor share of national income
items.take: Barr said the labor share of national income, steady at 60% to 65% after World War II, began falling in 2001 and reached a record low of 52.8% in Q2 2026. He cited three causes from economic research: technology that reduced labor demand, concentrated market power in many industries, and weaker worker bargaining power. AlphaGen read: he ties each cause to how AI may affect inequality, so the labor share is a variable he is tracking for the outlook.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Barr speech

items.headline: Housing starts 1.221M in September, down three straight months; permits 1.398M
items.take: Census data on FRED show housing starts at 1.221 million annualized in September, down from 1.288 million in August, 1.369 million in July and 1.439 million in June, 15.1% below June by our calculation. Building permits were 1.398 million in September, 177,000 or 14.5% above starts. The Census schedule lists October starts and permits for Nov. 18 at 8:30 a.m. ET. AlphaGen read: permits holding near 1.4 million while starts fall leaves a gap the October data will test.
items.source_name: U.S. Census Bureau via FRED

items.headline: Payrolls rose 401,000 over four months to October, averaging 100,250 a month
items.take: FRED's total nonfarm payroll series (PAYEMS) rose from 158,892 thousand in June to 159,293 thousand in October, a gain of 401,000, or 100,250 a month. Monthly changes were -10,000 in July, +186,000 in August, +60,000 in September and +165,000 in October. AlphaGen read: the four-month average smooths one negative month, July, in an otherwise positive run.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (PAYEMS)

items.headline: Unemployment rate 4.1% in October, within a 4.1%-4.2% range for five months
items.take: FRED shows the unemployment rate at 4.1% in October, after 4.2% in September, 4.1% in both July and August, and 4.2% in June. It was 4.3% in each of March, April and May. AlphaGen read: the rate has moved no more than 0.1 point a month since June, so October's reading continues a flat pattern rather than breaking it.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (UNRATE)

items.headline: Retail sales $745.0B in September, 6.1% above January; up in 7 of 8 months
items.take: FRED's advance retail and food services sales series (RSAFS) was $745,021 million in September versus $701,860 million in January, a 6.1% rise, and 1.7% above June's $732,898 million. Sales rose in seven of the eight month-to-month changes from January to September; the exception was July, at $729,915 million. These are dollar amounts not adjusted for price changes.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (RSAFS)

items.headline: 30-year mortgage rate 7.18% on Nov. 5, 0.47 point above Sept. 3 after 7.40% peak
items.take: Freddie Mac's weekly 30-year fixed rate, via FRED, was 7.18% for the week of Nov. 5 versus 6.71% on Sept. 3, a rise of 0.47 percentage point. It climbed to 7.40% on Oct. 8 and Oct. 15, then fell 0.22 point to the latest reading over three weeks. AlphaGen read: borrowers have recovered under half of the 0.69-point September-October increase.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (MORTGAGE30US)

items.headline: Brent spot $107.03 on Nov. 3, $28.48 below its Oct. 2 reading of $135.51
items.take: FRED's daily Brent spot series shows $107.03 per barrel on Nov. 3 versus $135.51 on Oct. 2, the highest daily reading in the series in October, a drop of $28.48. WTI was $99.64 on Nov. 3. The latest observation in the series is Nov. 3. AlphaGen read: the gap to the October high is large, but Brent is still above $100.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (DCOILBRENTEU)

items.headline: High-yield spread 3.30 points on Nov. 11, from 3.34; investment grade 0.90
items.take: FRED's ICE BofA option-adjusted spread for U.S. high-yield bonds was 3.30 percentage points on Nov. 11, down from 3.34 on Nov. 9 and 3.40 on Nov. 3. The investment-grade spread was 0.90, from 0.91 on Nov. 9 and 0.93 on Nov. 3. AlphaGen read: both gauges of extra yield over Treasuries edged lower, a sign of little added stress in corporate credit.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (BAMLH0A0HYM2, BAMLC0A0CM)

items.headline: CCC spread 13.30 points on Nov. 11 from 13.11, while BB narrows to 1.93
items.take: FRED shows the ICE BofA CCC-and-lower option-adjusted spread at 13.30 percentage points on Nov. 11, up from 13.11 on Nov. 9. Over the same dates the BB spread narrowed to 1.93 from 2.00 and the BBB spread to 1.12 from 1.13. AlphaGen read: the move was uneven, with the weakest-rated bonds widening while higher-rated tiers tightened.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (BAMLH0A3HYC, BAMLH0A1HYBB, BAMLC0A4CBBB)

items.headline: October payroll gain of 165,000 is 3.4 times the 48,000 prior 12-month average
items.take: BLS reported total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. The unemployment rate was 4.1 percent. AlphaGen read: the October gain is about 3.4 times the trailing monthly average, so one strong month stands out against a much slower year.
items.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Situation

items.headline: Existing-home sales 3.99M rate in September vs 4.08M a year earlier, down 2.2%
items.take: FRED's seasonally adjusted existing-home sales series stood at 3.99 million annual rate in September 2026, compared with 4.08 million in September 2025, a decline of 2.2%. It was 3.93 million in August 2026. AlphaGen read: sales improved from August but remain below the level of a year ago.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (EXHOSLUSM495S)

items.headline: Initial jobless claims 200,000 in week ended Nov. 7, up from 191,000
items.take: FRED shows seasonally adjusted initial claims at 200,000 for the week ended Nov. 7, up from 191,000 the week before and 195,000 in each of the two weeks before that. The four-week average of the latest four weekly readings is 195,250. AlphaGen read: the rise reverses most of the prior week's dip, but claims remain close to the 191,000-200,000 range of the past six weeks.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (ICSA)

items.headline: U.S. regular gasoline averages $3.995 a gallon, down from $4.354 on Oct. 5
items.take: FRED's weekly U.S. regular gasoline series stood at $3.995 per gallon on Nov. 9, down from $4.153 on Nov. 2, $4.284 on Oct. 19 and $4.354 on Oct. 5, a fall of $0.359 over five weeks. The Nov. 9 figure is 30.7% above the $3.056 recorded on Nov. 10, 2025. AlphaGen read: pump prices have eased for four straight weeks but remain well above a year ago.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (GASREGW)

items.headline: SOFR 3.89% on Nov. 10, inside the 3.75%-4.00% fed funds target range
items.take: FRED shows the secured overnight financing rate at 3.89% on Nov. 10, up from 3.88% on Nov. 9 and down from 3.97% on Nov. 3. The target range for the federal funds rate is 3.75% to 4.00% as of Nov. 12, and the effective federal funds rate was 3.88% on Nov. 9. AlphaGen read: overnight repo funding is trading 14 basis points above the bottom of the range and 11 below the top, in line with the policy rate.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (SOFR)

items.headline: Invitation Homes adds Cousins Properties CEO Colin Connolly to its board
items.take: Invitation Homes said its board raised its size from 9 to 10 members and appointed M. Colin Connolly, President, CEO and a director of Cousins Properties, as a director effective Nov. 13, 2026, with a term running to the 2027 annual meeting. He joins the Compensation and Management Development and Investment and Finance committees and receives a one-time restricted stock unit award valued at $96,000. The filing states no arrangement under which he was selected, so the move reads as a routine governance addition rather than a strategy change.
items.source_name: SEC EDGAR, Invitation Homes Form 8-K

items.headline: September PPI: processed goods for intermediate demand +2.5%, 14.1% over 12 months
items.take: BLS says the index for processed goods for intermediate demand rose 2.5% in September, the largest rise since 2.8% in May, with more than 80% of the advance attributable to a 10.2% increase in processed energy goods. Nearly half of the rise traces to a 21.0% increase in diesel fuel, and the 12-month increase of 14.1% is the largest since 14.3% in August 2022. AlphaGen read: input costs further up the supply chain were rising faster than final-demand prices in the latest PPI (released Oct. 15); the October report is due Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: September PPI: unprocessed intermediate goods +8.4%, crude petroleum +28.3%
items.take: BLS says prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand rose 8.4% in September, the largest increase since 9.2% in February 2022, and are up 21.5% for the 12 months ended in September. Over 80% of the September advance is attributable to unprocessed energy materials, which jumped 22.2%, led by a 28.3% rise in crude petroleum. AlphaGen read: this is the earliest stage of the PPI pipeline, and it shows the September price surge was concentrated in crude oil.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: September PPI: services for intermediate demand +0.9%, trade margins +2.0%
items.take: BLS says the index for services for intermediate demand rose 0.9% in September, matching the largest increase since 0.9% in April, with over 40% of the advance traced to a 2.0% jump in trade-services margins. Transportation and warehousing services rose 1.8%, and the index is up 6.3% over the 12 months ended in September, the largest 12-month advance since 6.3% in January 2023. AlphaGen read: business-to-business service prices, not just fuel, were climbing in the latest PPI (released Oct. 15).
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: Fed target range 3.75%-4.00%, ECB deposit rate 2.50%: both raised in September
items.take: FRED shows the ECB deposit facility rate at 2.50% on Nov. 11, up from 2.25% on Sept. 16, while the Federal Reserve's federal funds target range was 3.75% to 4.00% on Nov. 11, moved up from 3.50% to 3.75% on Sept. 17. The Fed's upper bound sits 1.50 percentage points above the ECB rate and its lower bound 1.25 points above. AlphaGen read: the two central banks made their latest moves a day apart, and the Fed's range remains 1.25 to 1.50 points above the ECB rate.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (ECB, Federal Reserve Board)

items.headline: September PPI final demand +1.3%, largest rise since March 2022; 6.3% over 12 months
items.take: BLS says the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 1.3% in September (seasonally adjusted) after 0.5% in August and 0.2% in July. On an unadjusted basis the index climbed 6.3% for the 12 months ended in September, the largest 12-month increase since 6.4% in December 2022. AlphaGen read: this September report, published Oct. 15, is the latest PPI in BLS's file and sets the bar the next report will be judged against.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: September PPI: final demand energy +10.8%; gasoline +20.3% drives half the goods rise
items.take: BLS says final demand goods prices rose 2.6% in September, the largest increase since the data were first calculated in December 2009, and more than 80% of the rise is attributable to final demand energy, which jumped 10.8%. Half of the goods increase traces to gasoline, up 20.3%, with diesel fuel, jet fuel, residential electric power and crude petroleum also higher. AlphaGen read: the producer-price surge in September was mainly an energy story.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: September PPI services +0.8%: trade margins +1.4%, transportation and warehousing +3.4%
items.take: BLS says final demand services prices rose 0.8% in September, the largest rise since a 0.8% gain in April. Nearly half of the increase is attributable to a 1.4% rise in margins for final demand trade services, while transportation and warehousing services rose 3.4% and services less trade, transportation and warehousing rose 0.3%. Margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling advanced 3.9%, while margins for automotive fuels and lubricants retailing dropped 30.3%.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: September PPI excluding food, energy and trade +0.5%, 5.0% over 12 months; foods +1.2%
items.take: BLS says final demand less foods, energy and trade services rose 0.5% in September after 0.3% in August, and 5.0% for the 12 months ended in September. Final demand foods rose 1.2% and goods less foods and energy rose 0.3%, while chicken egg prices dropped 39.7%. AlphaGen read: the narrower measure also accelerated, so the September jump was not confined to energy.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index

items.headline: CPI owners' equivalent rent +0.3%, rent +0.2% in October; lodging away from home +0.6%
items.take: BLS says the shelter index rose 0.3% in October after 0.4% in September, with owners' equivalent rent up 0.3% and rent up 0.2%. Lodging away from home rose 0.6% after a 2.0% increase the previous month. AlphaGen read: the monthly shelter gain slowed from September, while lodging remains the volatile piece.
items.source_name: BLS, Consumer Price Index

items.headline: CPI used cars and trucks -1.2% in October, -3.3% over 12 months; new vehicles +0.2%
items.take: BLS reports the used cars and trucks index fell 1.2% in October after rising 0.7% in September, and is down 3.3% over the 12 months ended October on an unadjusted basis. New vehicles rose 0.2%, matching September, and are up 0.7% on the year. AlphaGen read: vehicles are pulling in opposite directions, with used cars falling while new vehicles rose.
items.source_name: BLS, Consumer Price Index

items.headline: CPI recreation index +0.8% in October after +0.5%; motor vehicle insurance +0.7%
items.take: BLS says the recreation index rose 0.8% in October after 0.5% in September, while motor vehicle insurance rose 0.7%, household furnishings and operations 0.2% and education 0.3%. The communication index fell 0.1%. AlphaGen read: services outside shelter, led by recreation, contributed to the 0.3% core gain.
items.source_name: BLS, Consumer Price Index

items.headline: CPI gasoline +1.0% seasonally adjusted in October, but down 0.7% before adjustment
items.take: BLS says the gasoline index rose 1.0% in October after advancing 9.1% in September; before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices decreased 0.7%. Electricity rose 0.9% and the natural gas index fell 0.8% in the month. AlphaGen read: the seasonal factors turned an unadjusted decline into a gain in the gasoline index.
items.source_name: BLS, Consumer Price Index

items.headline: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread 0.25 point on Nov. 10, from 0.32 on Nov. 9
items.take: FRED shows the 10-year minus 2-year Treasury constant-maturity spread at 0.25 percentage point on Nov. 10, down from 0.32 on Nov. 9 and 0.38 on Nov. 5. The spread remains positive. AlphaGen read: the curve flattened over the week, the opposite of the widening in the Oct. 28 H.15 data.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Invesco QQQ AUM $463.8B at Oct. 31 vs $498.9B; Global Liquidity $230.0B vs $261.6B
items.take: Invesco's preliminary Oct. 31 assets under management table shows QQQ at $463.8 billion versus $498.9 billion at Sept. 30, a $35.1 billion decline of 7.0%, and Global Liquidity at $230.0 billion versus $261.6 billion, down $31.6 billion or 12.1%. Invesco said October numbers are preliminary and subject to adjustment. AlphaGen read: those two lines account for most of the $84.3 billion drop in total AUM to $2,453.5 billion.
items.source_name: SEC EDGAR, IVZ Form 8-K (Ex. 99.1)

items.headline: Bowman: October CPI suggests 12-month core PCE inflation likely rose to 3.3%
items.take: In her Nov. 10 speech, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman said the day's consumer price index suggests 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices. She said progress on lowering inflation has stalled over the past two years or so and that the latest data suggest price pressures may be broadening. AlphaGen read: her own forecast still has core PCE moving closer to 2 percent next year, so the worry is persistence, not a changed endpoint.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board speeches

items.headline: Bowman flags equity correction and sharp rise in long-term rates as growth risks
items.take: Bowman said she sees risks to economic activity originating in financial markets, including a large correction in equity valuations if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations and a sharp increase in private longer-term interest rates. She said lower equity prices could undermine resilience in consumer spending and higher rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors like housing and small business investment. AlphaGen read: she is naming the two channels, wealth effects and borrowing costs, that would link markets to the real economy.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board speeches

items.headline: Waller: uncertainty since early 2025 may be holding back hiring; cites Beige Book
items.take: Governor Waller said hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025, including the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and general uncertainty about the outlook. He cited the Fed's November 2025 Beige Book, where employers reported hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty, and the most recent Beige Book, where several Districts reported firms delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI. He said he does not think uncertainty has diminished much since then. AlphaGen read: he is treating part of the low-hire pattern as uncertainty-driven rather than purely structural.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board speeches

items.headline: Waller: low firing may partly reflect 2020-2023 job-switching surge, possibly temporary
items.take: Waller said low firing may be a consequence of the surge in job-switching from 2020 to 2023, since workers in new jobs are less inclined to change jobs again. He said that if this is a large factor it may be temporary, because workers stay in their jobs a median of three years before switching again and the last of the pandemic job switchers are nearing that threshold. AlphaGen read: this is the argument that labor-market dynamism could recover without a policy change.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board speeches

items.headline: Effective fed funds rate 3.88% is 0.76 point above 12-month core PCE inflation of 3.12%
items.take: FRED shows the effective federal funds rate (DFF) at 3.88% on Nov. 9, with the target range at 3.75% to 4.00%. Core PCE prices (PCEPILFE) were 3.12% above their September 2025 level in September 2026. The difference is 0.76 percentage point. AlphaGen's read: this is a simple gap between a nominal policy rate and a trailing inflation measure, not an official estimate of the real rate.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: 10-year Treasury yield 0.64 point above 3-month bill on Nov. 9, from 0.67 on Nov. 5
items.take: FRED data show the 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield at 4.88% and the 3-month yield at 4.24% on Nov. 9, a 0.64 percentage-point gap. On Nov. 5 the yields were 4.84% and 4.17%, a 0.67-point gap. AlphaGen's read: the 10-year yield remains above short-term bill yields, a positively sloped curve at that end.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Building permits 1.398M annual rate in September, down 0.4% from August
items.take: FRED's series for new private housing units authorized by building permits (PERMIT) stood at 1,398 thousand at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in September, against 1,403 thousand in August and 1,444 thousand in September 2025. That is 0.4% below August and 3.2% below a year earlier. AlphaGen's read: permits are a lead indicator for construction, and a flat-to-lower reading points to little near-term acceleration in new supply.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Core PCE price index up 2.9% annualized over three months vs 3.1% on the year
items.take: FRED's core PCE price index (PCEPILFE) reached 130.902 in September, from 129.969 in June and 126.940 in September 2025. That works out to a 2.90% annualized rate over the three months and 3.12% over twelve months. AlphaGen's read: the recent pace is slightly below the 12-month rate, so the three-month data do not show reacceleration.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Core CPI index up 0.30% in October; 3.7% annualized over three months
items.take: FRED's seasonally adjusted CPI excluding food and energy (CPILFESL) was 339.900 in October, against 338.896 in September and 336.789 in July. That is a 0.30% monthly rise and a 3.75% annualized pace over the three months from July. AlphaGen's read: the short-run pace is running above the 12-month core PCE rate of 3.12%, a reminder that the two inflation gauges differ in weights and coverage.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Atlanta Fed GDPNow shows 3.48% for Q4 vs 3.27% for Q3
items.take: FRED's GDPNow series, published by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, stands at 3.4810% for the quarter dated 2026-10-01, against 3.2721% for the quarter dated 2026-07-01 and 1.5400% for 2026-04-01. A nowcast is a model estimate that updates with each data release, not an official GDP figure. AlphaGen's read: a Q4 nowcast above the Q3 estimate points to growth holding up into year-end, though early-quarter nowcasts are revised often.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Global copper price $14,473 per tonne in September, up 44.8% from a year earlier
items.take: The global price of copper averaged $14,473.06 per metric ton in September 2026, from $14,331.26 in August and $9,994.77 in September 2025, a rise of 1.0% on the month and 44.8% on the year. AlphaGen's read: a 12-month gain this large keeps input costs elevated for wiring, electrical equipment and construction.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Global aluminum price $3,283 per tonne in September, up 23.7% on the year
items.take: The global price of aluminum averaged $3,283.05 per metric ton in September 2026, from $3,250.12 in August and $2,654.48 in September 2025, a rise of 1.0% on the month and 23.7% on the year. AlphaGen's read: aluminum is above its year-ago level, which matters for packaging, autos and aerospace costs.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Global wheat price $247 per tonne in September, up 59% from a year earlier
items.take: The global price of wheat averaged $246.85 per metric ton in September 2026, from $237.86 in August and $155.12 in September 2025, a rise of 3.8% on the month and 59.1% on the year. AlphaGen's read: grain costs are an early input into food prices, so a gain of this size is worth tracking in upcoming CPI food readings.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Global maize price $237 per tonne in September, up 20.8% on the year
items.take: The global price of maize (corn) averaged $236.92 per metric ton in September 2026, from $221.30 in August and $196.15 in September 2025, a rise of 7.1% on the month and 20.8% on the year. AlphaGen's read: maize feeds livestock and ethanol as well as food, so higher prices spread across several cost lines.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Fed: Veterans Day holiday moves Nov. 11 statistical releases to Thursday, Nov. 12
items.take: The Federal Reserve Board's November calendar lists Nov. 11 as a holiday (Veterans Day) and says the daily and weekly statistical releases scheduled for that day will be released Thursday, Nov. 12. Nov. 12 also lists the 1:00 p.m. commercial paper release, the 4:15 p.m. H.15 selected interest rates and the 4:30 p.m. H.4.1 balance sheet release. AlphaGen read: the weekly Fed balance sheet and rates data arrive together on Thursday afternoon.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (calendar: November 2026)

items.headline: Fed calendar: Barr speaks Nov. 12; Bowman and Jefferson appear Nov. 13
items.take: The Federal Reserve Board's calendar lists Governor Michael S. Barr on "Artificial Intelligence and Inequality" at 10:00 a.m. on Nov. 12 (virtual), Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman in a discussion on "Supervision and Regulation" at 10:50 a.m. on Nov. 13 (Connecticut Bankers Association, virtual), and Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson on productivity puzzles at 7:00 p.m. on Nov. 13 in La Jolla, Calif. AlphaGen read: Jefferson's Friday-evening talk is the one scheduled appearance on the macroeconomic outlook.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (calendar: November 2026)

items.headline: Fed calendar: foreign exchange rates Nov. 16, industrial production Nov. 17
items.take: The Federal Reserve Board's calendar lists the H.10 foreign exchange rates release at 4:15 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 16 and the G.17 industrial production and capacity utilization release at 9:15 a.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 17. The calendar shows no speeches or testimony for Nov. 16-20. AlphaGen read: the G.17 is the next Fed data print on the schedule for the week after next.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (calendar: November 2026)

items.headline: 1-year Treasury yield 4.38% on Nov. 9, 0.50 point above 3.88% fed funds rate
items.take: The Fed's H.15 release shows the 1-year Treasury constant-maturity yield at 4.38% on Nov. 9, up from 4.28% on Nov. 5, with the 6-month at 4.26% and the 3-month at 4.24%. The effective federal funds rate was 3.88% on each day shown, so the 1-year yield was 0.50 point above it. AlphaGen read: short-dated yields sit above the policy rate and rose across Nov. 5-9.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (H.15 Selected Interest Rates)

items.headline: Treasury yields rose Nov. 5-9: 2-year +0.10 pt to 4.56%, 5-year +0.08 to 4.67%
items.take: H.15 shows the 2-year Treasury yield at 4.56% on Nov. 9 versus 4.46% on Nov. 5, the 5-year at 4.67% versus 4.59%, the 10-year at 4.88% versus 4.84%, and the 30-year at 5.26% versus 5.25%. The rise was largest at the front of the curve, 0.10 point at 2 years against 0.01 point at 30 years. AlphaGen read: the move flattened the 2-year-to-30-year gap to 0.70 point from 0.79.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board (H.15 Selected Interest Rates)

items.headline: 10-year breakeven inflation rate 2.20% on Nov. 10, from 2.30% on Nov. 3
items.take: The 10-year breakeven inflation rate was 2.20% on Nov. 10, per FRED, down from 2.22% on Nov. 9 and 2.30% on Nov. 3; it fell on each of the last five readings. AlphaGen read: 2.20% is the lowest of the six daily readings in the latest FRED pull.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED, T10YIE)

items.headline: Euro at $1.1154 on Nov. 6, from $1.1235 on Nov. 5 and $1.1163 on Oct. 30
items.take: The Federal Reserve's H.10 rate for the euro was $1.1154 on Nov. 6, per FRED, down from $1.1235 on Nov. 5 and $1.1163 on Oct. 30. AlphaGen read: the Nov. 6 reading is the lowest of the six in the latest FRED pull, which begins Oct. 30.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board via FRED (DEXUSEU)

items.headline: 2-year Treasury yield 0.68 point above SOFR on Nov. 9, from 0.64 on Nov. 2
items.take: The 2-year Treasury yield was 4.56% on Nov. 9 and SOFR was 3.88%, per FRED, a gap of 0.68 percentage point versus 0.64 on Nov. 2 (4.59% and 3.95%). AlphaGen read: the gap widened as SOFR fell 7 basis points while the 2-year yield dipped 3 basis points over the week.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED, DGS2 and SOFR)

items.headline: 30-year Treasury yield 0.38 point above the 10-year on Nov. 9; 5.26% vs 4.88%
items.take: The 30-year Treasury constant-maturity yield was 5.26% on Nov. 9 against 4.88% for the 10-year, per FRED, a 0.38 percentage point gap versus 0.37 on Nov. 2 (5.28% and 4.91%). AlphaGen read: both yields ended the week lower than Nov. 2, by 2 basis points for the 30-year and 3 for the 10-year, so the gap held nearly flat.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board via FRED (DGS30, DGS10)

items.headline: Industrial production index rose 0.66% in September, 2.25% above a year earlier
items.take: The Federal Reserve's industrial production index was 103.9506 in September, up from 103.2664 in August (+0.66%) and 101.668 in September 2025 (+2.25%), per FRED. The Fed's October reading is scheduled for Nov. 17 at 9:15 a.m. ET. AlphaGen read: factory and utility output has risen in each of the last four monthly readings on FRED.

items.take: In a Nov. 10 statement to the European Parliament's economic affairs committee, ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone said the Eurosystem's Pontes platform, launched in September, had 18 market participants and market DLT operators onboarded on day one. items.take: Cipollone said in July the ECB announced the 36 payment service providers selected for the digital euro pilot from more than 50 applicants, covering banks and non-bank providers. items.headline: ECB's Lane: speeches between meetings can move rates across maturities
items.take: In a Nov. 10 keynote at the Bank of England and its Watchers Conference, ECB Executive Board member Philip Lane cited research on thousands of speeches, interviews and hearings showing that communication between policy meetings can affect market interest rates across maturities. He said it can help markets anticipate policy changes, particularly ahead of tightening episodes, and that its cumulative effect over time can be comparable to that of policy announcements, especially at longer maturities. AlphaGen read: for rate-watchers, the ECB is saying a speech calendar matters between meetings, not only decision days.

items.headline: ECB's Cipollone backs mandatory cash acceptance; euro notes turn 25 in two months
items.take: Cipollone told the European Parliament committee on Nov. 10 that the ECB supports strong legislative provisions on mandatory cash acceptance, access to cash across the euro area and the resilience of cash infrastructure. He said that in two months the 25th anniversary of euro banknotes and coins entering circulation will be marked, and that adoption of the legal framework is necessary to issue a digital euro. AlphaGen read: the ECB is pairing its digital euro push with a cash-protection message to win legislative support.

items.take: In a Nov. 10 speech, Fed Governor Waller said the initial estimate was that real GDP rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, with consumption 'helped by a booming stock market' and business investment continuing to surge, especially in high-tech equipment tied to the AI buildout. He said he expects growth to back off a bit in the current quarter as consumer spending slows to levels he thinks are more consistent with household income and wealth, while output keeps growing at a solid pace. items.headline: Waller: aging, education explain part of low dynamism; degree share 28% to 37%
items.take: Waller said part of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect longer-run trends that predate the pandemic: an aging workforce, since older workers switch jobs less often, and rising education, since the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent in 2010 to 37 percent. He said that if those were the only reasons, dynamism would be at a level consistent with trend, with no implications for monetary policy, but said that even after accounting for them, dynamism still seems somewhat low. AlphaGen read: the speech separates structural drift from cyclical weakness, which is the distinction that matters for policy.
